title: How to Build an App With AI: A Practical Guide From Idea to Working Software
description: Learn how to build an app with AI through a complete client-request tracker example, from a clear brief to data, testing, and deployment.
intro: To build an app with AI, define one useful workflow, describe its records and rules, generate a small working slice, and test the full action before expanding. Connect real persistence and integrations deliberately, then verify the published version. This tutorial uses a fictional client-request tracker to show what to ask for, what to check, and how to recover when the first attempt is wrong.

sections.heading: Choose one user and one useful outcome
paragraphs: Begin with a person doing a task rather than a list of features. In this tutorial, a small creative studio needs to collect client requests and move them through a clear review process. Today those requests are scattered across email. The first app will let a client submit a request, let a coordinator review it, and show an understandable status. It will not replace the studio's entire operating system.

Write a sentence you can test: a client can submit a request and later see whether it is received, in progress, waiting for information, or completed. This sentence implies an input, a saved record, authorized access, and a visible result. It is already more useful than asking for a beautiful client portal. A visual style can be chosen later without changing the main outcome.

Pick a project whose behavior you can explain. If you understand the studio's request process, you can recognize when the builder invents a confusing status or permits the wrong action. AI can help implement and refine the software, but your knowledge of the user's task provides the standard for judging it. A specific outcome keeps both the generation and your feedback grounded.

sections.heading: Decide what the first version excludes
paragraphs: Exclusions are part of a useful specification. The request tracker will not include invoices, online payment, public comments, automated file processing, or an AI assistant inside the finished app. Those features may become useful later, but each introduces its own behavior and operational dependencies. Adding them now would make it harder to learn whether clients understand the central request flow.

Also distinguish a prototype from a pilot. A prototype may use fictional records to explore the interface. A pilot lets a limited, appropriate audience rely on a defined working flow. The prototype can be valuable without being ready for real client information. State which stage you are building so temporary elements remain visible instead of being mistaken for finished infrastructure.

A small first version is not a weak product. It is a manageable hypothesis. If clients cannot describe their request clearly or coordinators do not use the status view, a larger feature set will not solve the underlying problem. Establish a narrow finish line and improve it through observed use. The best next feature becomes easier to identify once the core action works.

sections.heading: Write the data model in ordinary language
paragraphs: The example app needs users, projects, and requests. A request belongs to one project and has a title, description, status, creator, creation time, and last-update time. A project belongs to a client organization. A coordinator can work on the projects assigned to them. These relationships are product rules before they are database tables.

Define a few field rules. A title is required and should have a reasonable length limit. A description can contain several paragraphs. Status must come from an explicit set rather than arbitrary text. The creation time is assigned by the system. If a request is completed, decide whether a client can reopen it or must create a new request. Ambiguous rules become inconsistent behavior when screens are generated separately.

Use fictional examples to make the model concrete. A project called Northstar Website might contain a request titled Replace the event banner, with status received. A second project might have no requests. A third might contain a long description. These examples help the builder create meaningful empty states and prevent every screen from depending on the same idealized sample record.

sections.heading: Define roles and visibility
paragraphs: The client can create a request within an accessible project and read the status of that request. The coordinator can update its status and add a response visible to the client. The owner can manage project access. Specify whether a client sees every request in their organization or only the requests they created. Either policy may be reasonable, but the application needs one clear answer.

Describe what happens when access is missing. A client opening another organization's request should receive an appropriate unavailable or access-denied result without exposing the private record. A removed coordinator should lose the relevant access. These requirements need to be enforced by the server or database rules handling the data, as well as reflected in the interface. Hiding a navigation item is insufficient.

For the first prototype, you can explore these roles with clearly labeled fictional examples. Before a pilot, verify them with properly separated test accounts. Keep a record of the checks and their outcomes. Role design is not an optional polish step that follows launch; it determines whether the app's central action is correct for each person using it.

sections.heading: Choose a suitable builder and project path
paragraphs: Choose a tool that supports the platform, data mechanism, repository arrangement, and publishing path you need. For a browser-based client portal, focus on web application capabilities. If you already have a studio website repository, decide whether this app should extend it or live as a separate project. Ask the builder to inspect existing conventions before changing established software.

A browser-first builder may simplify starting a new app. A repository-aware workflow can be useful when source history, existing architecture, and project-defined checks are central. An integrated cloud environment may reduce setup for a particular stack. Compare the actual supported path and current plan. A general recommendation cannot replace checking whether the relevant operation is available in your account.

In Xroga, begin with the written brief and identify the intended repository if one exists. Ask for an implementation plan tied to the current project and request clear verification evidence. The same discipline applies in other tools. The builder should help you make progress while preserving a coherent explanation of what was created, what was tested, and which external steps remain.

sections.heading: Use a first prompt that describes behavior
paragraphs: A starting prompt could read: Build a responsive web app for a small creative studio to collect client requests. The main workflow is client submission, coordinator review, and client status tracking. Start with a small prototype using fictional records. Use the existing project conventions if a repository is connected. Explain the proposed record model and the smallest working slice before adding external services.

Then specify the first slice: create a request form with title and description, validate required fields, save through the selected persistence mechanism, and show the saved request in a list. Include loading, empty, and failure states. Do not add payments, automated email, or file uploads yet. Keep the result usable on a phone. State any assumption that prevents you from completing the real flow.

This prompt does not guarantee a correct result. It makes the target easier to evaluate. Read the plan and correct misunderstandings before broad implementation. If the builder proposes five dashboards and a subscription system, bring it back to the client-request loop. Clear scope gives you a useful basis for feedback without needing to dictate every file or function.

sections.heading: Inspect the first interface with realistic content
paragraphs: Before connecting private services, examine the generated form and list using the fictional records. Does the form explain what a useful request contains? Is the status understandable? Can a client distinguish a new request from a completed one? Realistic wording reveals interface problems that placeholder text hides. A polished card with no meaningful content is difficult to evaluate.

Try unusual but plausible input. Enter a long title, a multi-paragraph description, punctuation, and a name that does not fit the builder's sample. Leave required fields empty. Narrow the screen. The application should explain how to correct input without discarding everything already typed. If it cannot handle these simple cases, fix the interaction before attaching real client work to it.

Give focused feedback. For example: the submit button remains active while the save is pending, so a client can accidentally submit twice; disable or safely handle repeat submission and show clear progress. That request describes an observable problem and a testable outcome. It is more useful than asking the builder to make the form professional or enterprise-ready.

sections.heading: Connect persistence deliberately
paragraphs: Ask the builder to identify where requests are stored. The answer should distinguish component state, browser storage, and a shared server database. The tutorial's eventual pilot needs a shared authoritative store because clients and coordinators use different sessions. A local demonstration can be a useful intermediate step if it is labeled and does not imply shared behavior it cannot provide.

Define what happens after saving. The server should confirm the saved record, the interface should show the resulting state, and a failed save should preserve the form with a helpful message. Test the action after a full reload. Then check it from the other relevant role in the test environment. Seeing the record immediately after a button click does not prove it was durably stored.

If you use Supabase, follow its documented access-control model and inspect the actual policies created for your tables. The general principle is to enforce who may read or change each record at the data boundary. Keep privileged credentials on trusted server paths. The implementation must be reviewed in the context of your app; connecting a database by itself does not establish correct authorization.

sections.heading: Add authentication after the basic flow is clear
paragraphs: Once the request model and form behavior are understandable, connect the supported authentication path needed for the pilot. Choose only the sign-in methods the audience needs. Verify registration or invitation, sign-in, session expiry, sign-out, and recovery through an appropriate test arrangement. A successful login is one part of the experience, not the complete account lifecycle.

Associate requests with identity using trusted session information. Do not let the browser decide ownership by submitting an arbitrary user identifier. Explain this requirement in plain language to the builder: a person must not be able to create a request as another client or select a private project by changing a request parameter. Then ask how that rule is enforced and tested.

Keep authentication changes separate from unrelated redesigns. If something breaks, you want to know which behavior changed. Recheck the original request-creation flow after adding sessions. Confirm that a signed-out visitor receives a clear next step instead of a blank page or an indefinite spinner. The interface should make an unavailable session understandable without exposing internal diagnostic details.

sections.heading: Implement a useful status lifecycle
paragraphs: A status lifecycle describes allowed movement between states. For this app, received means the studio has the request, in progress means work has started, waiting for information means the client needs to respond, and completed means the coordinator considers the work finished. Write those definitions down. If people interpret the same status differently, the app will create confusion even when its code behaves consistently.

Decide which transitions are allowed and who can make them. A client may add clarification while a coordinator changes progress status. If completion can be reversed, define the reopening action. Preserve relevant history when it matters to the workflow. You do not need an elaborate event system for every prototype, but you should avoid silently replacing information that users need to understand the current state.

Test a full lifecycle with one fictional request. Submit it, begin work, request clarification, respond, and complete it. Check the displayed text at each stage from both sides. This exercise often reveals a missing action or an ambiguous message. Fix those gaps before adding charts that summarize the statuses. A correct summary depends on correct underlying state changes.

sections.heading: Add search and filters after records exist
paragraphs: A request list becomes more useful when clients and coordinators can find the relevant work. Start with a few filters that match actual decisions, such as status and project. Search might cover request titles and descriptions. Define whether archived projects are included and how empty results differ from an empty account. The distinction helps users know whether they should change a filter or create a record.

Test filtering against a small dataset with known expected results. Include requests with similar titles, different projects, and different statuses. Combine filters and clear them. Refresh a filtered view if shareable URLs are part of the requirement. A filter that appears to work with one sample record may fail when categories overlap or a record changes status.

Avoid optimizing for a huge hypothetical dataset before you understand the actual usage. At the same time, ask the builder to avoid loading every private record into the browser merely to hide most of them. The data request should respect access rules and the intended scale. Use measurements from the working app to decide when pagination, indexing, or a different query strategy becomes necessary.

sections.heading: Treat external services as separate milestones
paragraphs: Suppose the studio later wants an email when a request is received. Define the event, recipient, template, duplicate behavior, and failure handling. An email integration needs more than a provider key and a button. Decide whether saving a request depends on delivery or whether the app records the request and reports notification status separately. The latter can be more resilient when the email provider is temporarily unavailable.

Test using the provider's appropriate test capabilities and approved addresses. Confirm the actual provider result and the visible application state. If a message is queued, label it queued rather than delivered. Keep secret values out of client bundles, public logs, and prompts. Record the configuration names and the responsible account so a future maintainer understands how the feature operates.

Add one integration at a time. File uploads, calendar events, and payments each deserve their own acceptance criteria. A successful request tracker does not become more useful simply because it displays more service logos. Choose the next integration based on a demonstrated user need, then verify its complete lifecycle rather than assuming the first successful request covers every later case.

sections.heading: Test failure paths before inviting clients
paragraphs: List the failures that would confuse or harm the user. A save might time out, a session might expire, a project might become unavailable, or a coordinator might edit a request while the client is viewing it. Decide what the interface should do in each case. The objective is not to predict every possible outage; it is to make common interruptions understandable and recoverable.

Test a failed save without losing the entered description. Check that a repeated click does not create confusing duplicates. Verify that a client cannot read another organization's request. Test a deep link after sign-out. Use a test environment and fictional records for these checks. Keep expected and actual results in a short checklist so you can repeat the relevant cases after changes.

When a check fails, report the actual failure to the builder. Include the starting state and the smallest sequence that reproduces it. Ask for a focused correction and a regression check. Avoid saying fix everything, which gives little direction and encourages broad changes. A small reproducible bug is easier to diagnose, verify, and explain than a general impression that the app feels broken.

sections.heading: Make the main journey accessible
paragraphs: A client should be able to complete the request flow without relying on tiny controls, color alone, or precise mouse movement. Label form fields clearly. Explain errors near the relevant input. Make focus visible and preserve a sensible keyboard order. Use headings that describe the content. These choices improve the experience for many users, including people on phones or working in distracting environments.

Check long descriptions and narrow screens. A status label should remain readable when translated or enlarged. A dialog should not trap the user without an understandable close action. If the form fails, focus or announce the useful error rather than leaving the user to guess. Automated checks can help identify some issues, but completing the journey manually remains valuable.

Ask for concrete improvements. Say that the status is currently communicated only through a green dot and needs a written label. Say that the form error appears above the viewport on a phone. Recheck the specific problem after the change. Accessibility becomes more manageable when it is part of each working slice rather than an undefined final task after every feature has been added.

sections.heading: Prepare public pages for discovery
paragraphs: If the app has public explanatory pages, give each one a useful purpose and a stable URL. Make the main copy available as readable HTML, use descriptive headings and links, and provide accurate title and description metadata. Keep private client dashboards separate from public search content. A sitemap is a discovery aid for public pages, not a place to list private request records.

For the studio example, a public page might explain how the request process works, while the request list remains behind authentication. Do not publish fictional customer quotes or invented success statistics to make the page more persuasive. Use real product explanations and clearly labeled examples. A visitor should understand what the app does before deciding whether to sign in or contact the studio.

Search visibility is a separate outcome from publishing. Verify that the public URL works, that crawling is allowed where intended, and that the page has internal links. Google does not guarantee indexing or ranking. Focus on a useful page and a sound technical foundation, then use the site's own search-performance data to learn which questions people actually bring to it.

sections.heading: Deploy a version you can identify
paragraphs: A deployment should have an identifiable source version, target environment, and public address. Before publishing, run the project's appropriate checks and production build. Review required configuration names and verify which values belong in the production environment. A development preview can work while a production build fails, so do not substitute one for the other.

After deployment, open the intended URL in a fresh session. Load a deep link, sign in through the test path if relevant, submit a fictional request in the appropriate environment, and check the resulting record from the coordinator side. Confirm that the deployed version matches the change you intended to release. A provider status of ready is useful but does not prove the full user journey.

Keep the previous working version and the rollback path documented. If there are database changes, understand whether reverting code is compatible with the current data. For this tutorial, prefer additive, small changes and avoid destructive migrations. The goal is a release you can inspect and recover, not a dramatic publishing event that leaves the team unsure how to correct the next problem.

sections.heading: Collect feedback through tasks
paragraphs: Ask a small, appropriate pilot audience to submit a request and check its status. Observe completion, confusion, and errors. Ask what they expected at the point of hesitation. General questions such as do you like the portal can produce polite but unhelpful answers. A task gives you behavior you can act on and a clearer distinction between an interface problem and a missing feature.

Keep feedback attached to the relevant version and journey. If a client says a request disappeared, record which project, which action, and which status were involved using a privacy-conscious process. Do not paste private client descriptions into broad debugging prompts. Reproduce the issue with fictional content whenever possible. This gives the builder useful context while keeping the investigation focused.

Choose the next improvement based on the repeated obstacle that matters most. It may be a clearer field description, a better empty state, or a reliable notification, rather than a new dashboard. Make one change and repeat the task. AI can make implementation fast enough that restraint becomes an important product skill: use that speed to test a clear idea, not to multiply unverified features.

sections.heading: Maintain a short project memory
paragraphs: Keep a README or equivalent project note describing the app's purpose, setup, roles, data model, configuration names, and release process. Add a small list of known limitations and the next intended change. The note should reflect the actual application, not an optimistic roadmap. Update it when behavior changes. Future prompts and future maintainers both benefit from a concise factual reference.

Record the evidence for important milestones. A useful entry might identify the commit, passing build, tested request lifecycle, and published version. Another entry may state that email remains unconfigured. Both are valuable. Separating completed work from external setup prevents later sessions from treating an interface placeholder as a finished integration. It also reduces repeated investigation.

Keep changes reviewable. If a new prompt proposes replacing the data layer to adjust a label, investigate why. Broad rewrites can discard working behavior and make the project harder to understand. A maintainable AI-built app has the same advantage as any maintainable app: a person can explain its important parts, reproduce a problem, and make a bounded improvement with confidence.

sections.heading: Common mistakes and how to recover
paragraphs: If the app looks finished but saves nothing, identify the actual storage mechanism and implement one complete persistence path. If the builder keeps redesigning working screens, narrow the next prompt to a specific behavior and name what should remain intact. If every repair creates another unrelated failure, return to the last known working version and reproduce the smallest failing case.

If the project has too many unfinished features, write an inventory of real behavior. Mark each feature working, partially working, demonstration-only, or untested. Select one central user journey and complete it before continuing. This is often faster than trying to fix a large unfinished application through one enormous prompt. Clarity about state turns a confusing project into a sequence of manageable tasks.

If a required integration is unsupported, say so and choose a realistic alternative. You may simplify the first release, use a documented provider path, or involve a developer. More prompting cannot create account permissions or complete an external review that has not happened. A truthful blocker keeps the project recoverable and helps you make the next decision without building on a false assumption.

sections.heading: Walk through the request tracker with a small fixture
paragraphs: Create three fictional projects: Northstar Website, Elm Workshop, and Harbor Newsletter. Give Northstar two requests, Elm one, and Harbor none. Use different statuses and description lengths. Include one request that waits for information. This fixture is small enough that you can know the expected result of every filter and access rule without relying on a large dashboard to tell you what should happen.

Sign in through the appropriate test path as the Northstar client. Submit Replace the event banner with a short description and confirm that it appears in Northstar. Refresh and return through a direct link. Then use the coordinator view to change the status to waiting for information and add a clear question. The client should see the question and the accurate status, without seeing Elm's request.

Next, inspect Harbor's empty state. It should explain how to create the first request, not imply a network failure. Apply a completed filter to Northstar when no request is completed. That should produce a different message explaining that no records match the filter. These small distinctions make the app easier to understand and give you concrete behavior to verify after later changes.

sections.heading: Turn the brief into an acceptance worksheet
paragraphs: Write one row per observable behavior. Suggested rows include creating a valid request, rejecting an empty title, preserving a description after a failed save, showing a saved request after refresh, limiting access to the correct project, changing a status, and displaying the change in the client view. Add the starting state, steps, expected result, actual result, environment, and version.

Use plain pass, fail, or not tested states. Do not count an untested integration as passing because its button exists. When a row fails, attach the smallest safe reproduction and return it to the builder. If the app cannot be exercised because a provider is unavailable, record that as a configuration blocker. The worksheet should reflect what you observed, not what the generated summary says was intended.

After a focused correction, repeat the failed row and the related working path. For example, fixing status updates should not prevent new requests from being created. You do not need to repeat unrelated visual checks after every server change unless there is a reason, but you do need to protect the shared behavior the change touches. A compact worksheet makes that judgement more deliberate.

sections.heading: Add a feature through a bounded second release
paragraphs: Suppose pilot users repeatedly ask for an attachment on a request. Begin by defining the actual need: one image illustrating a visual change, rather than arbitrary large files. Decide which file types and sizes are supported, who can view them, and what happens when an upload fails. Determine whether the request can be saved without the attachment. These decisions should precede the storage integration.

Ask the builder to use the project's existing upload patterns if they exist. Keep file access aligned with project access. A request image should not become publicly readable merely because its storage URL is convenient. Use fictional images in testing and verify the result from the client and coordinator views. A successful upload from one account does not establish correct access from another.

Release the attachment feature separately from a major redesign or a new notification system. That makes its effect easier to understand. Update the brief, the data explanation, and the acceptance worksheet. If the feature proves unnecessary or creates more confusion than value, you can simplify it without discarding the working request tracker. Bounded releases let the product evolve while preserving what users already understand.

sections.heading: Understand the difference between app-building AI and in-app AI
paragraphs: An app built with AI does not have to contain an AI feature. The request tracker can be useful with ordinary forms, records, and status changes. The builder helps create and maintain the software. An in-app AI feature, such as summarizing a request, would be a separate product capability with its own provider calls, data handling, failure behavior, and usage cost.

Add such a feature only when it improves a defined user task. If coordinators spend time reading very long requests, a draft summary might help. It should remain distinguishable from the original text and should not silently change the request or make an irreversible decision. Test it with representative fictional descriptions, including ambiguous and incomplete ones. Decide how users correct an inaccurate summary.

Account for runtime usage separately from building capacity. Every summary may consume model resources after the app is published. Establish appropriate limits and a clear fallback if the provider is unavailable. Avoid adding an AI chat box simply because the product was generated by AI. Useful application behavior comes from the user's need, and the simplest reliable feature may use no model at runtime at all.

sections.heading: Prepare a developer handoff when the project grows
paragraphs: A developer joining later needs the repository or supported export, the data model, role definitions, configuration names, test steps, and the observed problems. Provide the actual working version and explain which parts are prototypes. Do not send only screenshots and a request to make it production-ready. A specific handoff makes the review more focused and preserves the work that is already useful.

Ask for a bounded review first, such as checking the request access rules and deployment configuration. The reviewer can identify concrete gaps before proposing a larger rebuild. Some generated code may be entirely suitable; other parts may need correction. The decision should follow the implementation and requirements. AI-assisted creation and human review can fit within the same maintainable product workflow.

sections.heading: Frequently asked questions about building with AI
paragraphs: Can AI build an entire app? It can help create substantial parts of an application, and some projects can be taken through a complete supported build and deployment workflow. Success depends on the requirements, tools, permissions, configuration, and verification. Judge your application by its actual user journey rather than a general claim about what AI can do.

How long does it take? A small demonstration can be quick, while a dependable multi-user product needs time for domain decisions, data rules, testing, and operations. This tutorial provides a workflow, not a delivery-time guarantee. Estimate after defining the smallest release and identifying external dependencies. Treat unexpected complexity as information to investigate rather than a reason to hide unfinished work.

Should I start with design or data? Start with the user outcome, then sketch the records and the journey together. A lightweight interface helps expose confusing requirements, while the data model prevents screens from making incompatible assumptions. You can iterate between them. Avoid polishing a large interface before confirming how its central action will actually work.

What should I do next? Write a one-page brief for your own example, choose a suitable builder, and complete one vertical slice with fictional records. Verify saving, access, failure behavior, and a fresh-session preview. Then decide whether to add the next action or invite a bounded pilot audience. That sequence gives you working software and useful evidence at every stage.

title: AI App Builder Prompts: A Practical Framework and 20 Useful Examples
description: Use 20 AI app builder prompts for planning, data, design, debugging, testing, and publishing, with practical acceptance criteria for each.
intro: A useful AI app builder prompt describes the user, the task, the records, the constraints, and the evidence needed to accept the result. Start with one working flow, then use focused prompts for data, permissions, design, debugging, and release. The examples below are original templates to adapt to your project; they are not promises of one-prompt production software.

sections.heading: Why a clear prompt changes the build
paragraphs: A vague prompt leaves important decisions open. Build a professional app might mean a marketing page, an authenticated dashboard, or an entire operational system. The builder must choose an audience, invent records, decide which actions exist, and guess what completion means. Some guesses will be reasonable and others will be wrong. Better prompts reduce that uncertainty by making the product decisions visible.

Clarity does not mean writing the longest possible instruction. A short prompt with a defined outcome can be more useful than several pages of unrelated requirements. The goal is to supply the context needed for the next bounded step. Explain the behavior and constraints that distinguish your app from a generic example. Leave low-impact implementation choices open when the project already has appropriate conventions.

Official prompting guidance from Lovable and Bolt also emphasizes planning and clearer instructions. The framework here is a practical editorial method, not a proprietary formula from either product. Use it to organize your own requirements and assess the result. A good prompt improves the starting conditions; testing determines whether the resulting application actually satisfies them.

sections.heading: Use the five-part prompt framework
paragraphs: The first part is context: who uses the app and what problem they face. The second is outcome: the single task or change you want now. The third is the data and behavior: records, relationships, states, and important rules. The fourth is constraints: existing architecture, excluded features, supported providers, and permission boundaries. The fifth is acceptance: what you will observe to consider the step complete.

For example, a coworking manager needs to track meeting-room reservations. The next outcome is a usable reservation flow. The data includes rooms, time slots, members, and bookings. Constraints might exclude payments and automatic calendar synchronization in the prototype. Acceptance includes preventing overlapping bookings, displaying a clear error, and preserving saved reservations after refresh. Each part removes a different kind of ambiguity.

Keep the framework flexible. A small copy change does not need a database specification. A role-sensitive feature does need its access rules. When the project is unfamiliar, ask the builder to inspect the relevant files before proposing implementation. When a decision is genuinely missing, ask for the options and their effect. A prompt should guide a real task, not become a ritual that obscures it.

sections.heading: Supply context that can be trusted
paragraphs: Useful context includes a written workflow, representative fictional records, relevant source files, existing design conventions, and an observed error. Explain which information is a requirement and which is only a reference. A screenshot can show visual hierarchy without establishing that every displayed feature should be implemented. A competitor's page can inspire a question without granting permission to copy its wording or assets.

Avoid pasting entire repositories or long unrelated conversations when a few files answer the question. Too much irrelevant material can make the intended task harder to identify. Ask the builder to locate the actual route, component, or request handler when repository tools are available. Then supply the missing domain information that code inspection cannot reveal, such as why a coordinator needs a particular decision.

Do not include secret values in an ordinary prompt. Refer to configuration names and use the product's protected connection path for credentials. Use fictional customer records for examples. The builder usually needs to know the shape and meaning of the data, not a real person's private information. Good context is relevant, understandable, and appropriate to the task's actual boundary.

sections.heading: Prompt 1: turn an idea into a narrow brief
paragraphs: Prompt: I want to help a neighborhood workshop track tools borrowed by members. Turn this idea into a one-page product brief. Identify the primary user, one useful workflow, the minimum records, the important exceptions, and a testable first-release outcome. Separate essential requirements from later ideas. Ask only for missing decisions that materially change the workflow. Do not generate application code yet.

Use this when the idea is broad and the builder would otherwise invent the product. Read the brief as the person who understands the workflow. If the tool assumes members can borrow unlimited tools or remove records, correct those rules. The brief should expose domain decisions rather than bury them inside a polished implementation that is expensive to revise.

Acceptance: another person can read the brief and explain what the first version does, who it serves, and what is excluded. You should be able to write a short manual test from it. If the brief contains only broad claims such as seamless management, ask for concrete actions and records. Specificity at this stage saves later implementation and repair work.

sections.heading: Prompt 2: inspect an existing repository
paragraphs: Prompt: Inspect the existing repository before proposing changes. Identify the framework, the route for the tool-loan workflow, the current data mechanism, the relevant permission checks, and the available build and test commands. Read the files that support your explanation. Propose the smallest change needed to add an overdue filter. Preserve unrelated work and state any uncertainty about the active code path.

Use this when adding to existing software. The builder should ground its plan in real files rather than assume a fresh architecture. An overdue filter may depend on return state, due dates, time zones, and archived loans. If the proposed plan changes the entire data layer, ask why that is necessary. The scope should follow the requirement and the evidence found in the repository.

Acceptance: the explanation names the relevant files and describes the current behavior accurately enough for review. Unsupported assumptions remain visible. The proposed test covers both overdue and returned items. A confident plan with invented paths is not acceptable context for implementation. Correct the project understanding before allowing broad edits to follow from it.

sections.heading: Prompt 3: create the first working slice
paragraphs: Prompt: Implement one complete tool-loan flow. A coordinator selects an available tool, chooses a fictional member, enters a due date, and saves the loan. The saved record appears in the current-loans list and the tool becomes unavailable. Include required-field validation, a pending state, and a recoverable save error. Use the project's existing persistence and interface patterns. Exclude payments and email.

Use this after the records and rules are clear. The prompt connects an action to a durable result instead of asking for many disconnected screens. It also names the failure behavior. If persistence is not configured, the builder should report that boundary or produce a clearly labeled demonstration, rather than silently pretending an in-memory update is a saved shared record.

Acceptance: perform the flow, refresh, and check the resulting record through the appropriate second view. Try an invalid due date and a repeated submit. Verify that the tool's availability reflects the authoritative loan state. This is more informative than accepting a screenshot of the new form. A vertical slice gives subsequent prompts a working foundation.

sections.heading: Prompt 4: model records and relationships
paragraphs: Prompt: Explain and implement the minimum data model for tools, members, and loans. A tool can have many historical loans but at most one active loan. A loan has a due date and optional return time. Define required fields, ownership, uniqueness, and archive behavior. Use an additive change where possible and describe how existing records remain compatible. Do not remove data to make the model fit.

Use this when the interface has begun to obscure what information is actually stored. Ask for a plain-language explanation alongside the implementation. If the current project already has a model, inspect it first. A clean theoretical schema is less useful than a compatible change that preserves working records and clearly documents any migration requirement.

Acceptance: inspect representative records and test the core constraints through the real data path. Returned loans should remain historical without keeping a tool unavailable. An archived member should not accidentally erase useful loan history. Use a test environment for migration checks. The important evidence is the behavior of the actual app, not merely a generated schema diagram.

sections.heading: Prompt 5: define role rules
paragraphs: Prompt: Add the documented member and coordinator roles to the tool-loan flow. Members may read their own loans and public availability. Coordinators may create and return loans for the workshop they manage. Enforce access at the trusted data boundary as well as in the interface. Explain what identity is trusted. Test an ordinary member, another workshop's coordinator, and a signed-out request.

Use this when the app becomes multi-user or multi-organization. The role names should match the real workflow. Avoid using administrator as a catch-all substitute for several responsibilities. Ask whether a removed role takes effect promptly and how a direct request to an unauthorized record behaves. These details determine whether the interface's apparent permissions correspond to actual access.

Acceptance: positive cases work and negative cases fail without exposing the protected record. Record which test identity performed each action in an appropriate test setup. Do not infer authorization from a hidden button. If credentials or isolated accounts are unavailable, mark the check unverified and resolve that gap before relying on the feature for private production data.

sections.heading: Prompt 6: improve a screen without changing behavior
paragraphs: Prompt: Improve the current-loans screen using the existing design system. Make the primary action clear, group related information, show due dates consistently, and keep status understandable without color alone. Preserve the current routes, data queries, role rules, and save behavior. Use realistic long names and an empty state. Explain the visual changes and recheck the existing loan flow afterward.

Use this when the core behavior works but the presentation is difficult to scan. Describe the observed problem rather than only an aesthetic adjective. For example, coordinators cannot distinguish a due date from a loan date at a glance. The builder then has a meaningful design objective. A request for a premium look alone may produce decorative changes that leave the confusion untouched.

Acceptance: the relevant information is easier to find, and the original flow still passes. Compare the same representative records before and after. Test at the intended desktop and phone widths. A redesign should not quietly change the meaning of a status or remove a needed action. Keeping the behavior boundary explicit makes visual iteration safer and easier to evaluate.

sections.heading: Prompt 7: fix mobile overflow
paragraphs: Prompt: At a viewport width of 390 pixels, the current-loans table hides the return action and requires horizontal scrolling. Provide a readable mobile layout using existing styling conventions. Keep the tool name, borrower, due date, status, and return action available. Preserve the desktop layout where it already works. Check long content, keyboard focus, and the open form with the software keyboard present.

Use this after observing a specific responsive failure. Include the affected viewport and the action that becomes inaccessible. The builder can then choose an appropriate layout, such as cards or a carefully structured table, instead of shrinking every element until the text becomes unreadable. A smaller screenshot is not the same as a usable mobile workflow.

Acceptance: complete the return flow on the narrow layout, then recheck desktop and an intermediate width. Verify that labels remain associated with values. Check that the controls do not overlap and that the confirmation remains visible. If a screenshot is used as evidence, pair it with an interaction check. Appearance alone cannot prove the action remains usable.

sections.heading: Prompt 8: add useful empty and failure states
paragraphs: Prompt: Review the current-loans page for first use, no matching results, loading, and failed loading. Give each state a clear message and an appropriate next action. Distinguish no loans from no loans matching the selected filter. Preserve existing records and user input when a request fails. Avoid reporting success until the authoritative operation confirms it. Keep technical diagnostics out of the normal user message.

Use this when the interface only works with ideal sample data. Empty states tell people how to begin, while failure states explain how to recover. Without that distinction, a user may assume their records have disappeared when a network request simply failed. The words matter as much as the layout because they communicate the actual state of the application.

Acceptance: reproduce each state intentionally in a test setup. Verify that retry does not duplicate an operation and that clearing filters restores the expected list. Check a slow request as well as an immediate error. A spinner that never resolves is not a useful failure state. The app should make the next reasonable action understandable without requiring a support explanation.

sections.heading: Prompt 9: add a trustworthy filter
paragraphs: Prompt: Add an overdue filter to the current-loans list. Define overdue as an active loan whose due date is before the workshop's configured current date. Returned loans are excluded. Explain the time-zone assumption. Keep filtering within the current user's authorized records. Test an overdue active loan, a due-today loan, a future loan, a returned loan, and an empty result.

Use this when a seemingly small feature depends on business meaning. The definition of overdue should not vary between the list, the badge, and the summary count. If the app stores timestamps rather than dates, investigate how the comparison is made. A filter that works in one time zone can behave incorrectly near midnight elsewhere.

Acceptance: compare the result against a tiny fixture with known expected membership. Check the count and the displayed records together. Change a returned state and confirm the filter updates. The builder should identify its assumptions rather than quietly choose them. Precise definitions are especially valuable in dashboards, where an attractive summary can hide an incorrect calculation.

sections.heading: Prompt 10: debug one reproducible failure
paragraphs: Prompt: When I save a return for loan L-104 in the test dataset, the interface shows completed but the tool remains unavailable after refresh. Expected: the return is saved and availability reflects that no active loan remains. Inspect the save result and the query deriving availability. Reproduce the failure, identify its cause, make a focused fix, and rerun the loan-and-return regression flow.

Use this instead of saying the database is broken. Supply safe reproduction steps and distinguish the expected state from the actual state. If you do not know the failing layer, avoid prescribing one. The interface, server, database, and cache are possible boundaries, and evidence should determine which one is responsible. A guessed fix can add complexity without correcting the cause.

Acceptance: the original reproduction now behaves correctly, the saved record is authoritative, and the earlier loan flow still works. Ask what was changed and which checks were actually run. If the failure could not be reproduced, the builder should say so. A speculative edit should not be reported as a verified repair merely because it compiles.

sections.heading: Prompt 11: add an external integration
paragraphs: Prompt: Add a supported transactional-email notification when a coordinator records a new loan. Define the recipient from the authorized member record and use a clear template. Preserve the saved loan if email delivery fails, show notification status accurately, and avoid duplicate messages after retries. Keep credentials on protected server paths. Use the provider's test arrangement and report the actual provider result.

Use this when a real workflow needs communication. Identify the trigger and failure policy before implementation. If the provider is not connected, the correct result is a clear setup requirement. A generated email preview can help review wording, but it is not evidence that a message was sent or delivered. Treat those as different states in both the interface and your acceptance notes.

Acceptance: verify the complete test path and the failure path, including a retry. Confirm that the app does not send to an arbitrary address supplied by an untrusted request. Review the template with fictional data. A service logo and a saved key do not complete the integration. The useful milestone is a defined operation with observable results and recovery behavior.

sections.heading: Prompt 12: protect source and configuration
paragraphs: Prompt: Review the proposed changes for accidental inclusion of private configuration. List required environment-variable names and identify which are public or server-only. Use the existing protected configuration mechanism. Do not print secret values or place them in browser code, fixtures, screenshots, or committed files. If a required value is unavailable, report the exact configuration name and the blocked operation.

Use this around integrations and deployment changes. The prompt is not a substitute for secret scanning or code review, but it makes the expected handling explicit. Most implementation discussions need variable names and trust boundaries rather than credentials themselves. Keep the request scoped to the changed files and relevant runtime path, so the review remains actionable.

Acceptance: inspect the changed source and build configuration, run available relevant checks, and verify the feature through the appropriate environment. A statement that secrets are safe is not itself evidence. Conversely, the absence of a credential should not encourage a fake fallback that reports success. Clear blocked state is preferable to exposing sensitive configuration or masking an unavailable operation.

sections.heading: Prompt 13: prepare a production build
paragraphs: Prompt: Prepare this change for the project's existing production build. Use the declared toolchain and lockfile. Run the relevant tests and build commands, preserve the first meaningful failure, and fix only failures caused by this change. Identify required production configuration names. Report the source version, actual command results, and unresolved blockers. Do not treat a development preview as a passing production build.

Use this after the behavior is implemented and before release. Existing projects may have pre-existing warnings or unrelated failures. The report should distinguish them without suppressing a relevant failure. A focused change should not quietly upgrade major dependencies or rewrite the lockfile merely to make a command pass. Ask for the reasoning if the proposed repair expands scope.

Acceptance: the identified version passes the applicable checks, or the remaining blocker is reported accurately. Keep the output available for review. If an external credential is needed for a check, do not replace the check with a simulation and call it production evidence. Build success establishes buildability; deployment and the live user journey still need their own verification.

sections.heading: Prompt 14: verify a published version
paragraphs: Prompt: Verify the published version of this change at the intended environment. Confirm the deployment identity and source version, then open the URL in a fresh session and complete the authorized test journey with fictional records. Check deep-link loading, asset delivery, saving, and the relevant role boundary. Report what passed, what failed, and what was not tested. Preserve the previous working release reference.

Use this after the provider reports a deployment result. A ready status means something specific at the provider, but it does not prove that your application is configured correctly. A successful home-page request does not prove the loan flow. The prompt asks for evidence at the level of the intended outcome while keeping the test data and environment appropriate.

Acceptance: the expected change is visible and the relevant action works through the actual deployed path. Any missing test identity or unavailable integration remains a limitation. If the wrong version is deployed, resolve that before changing the code again. Confusing source state with production state can waste several rounds of prompting on a problem that is really release configuration.

sections.heading: Prompt 15: improve public-page search basics
paragraphs: Prompt: Improve the public guide page for its actual topic. Use one descriptive main heading, helpful visible text, a unique title and description, a canonical URL, and crawlable internal links. Ensure the page returns meaningful content without a login. Add accurate structured data only where it matches the visible content. Include the public canonical URL in the existing sitemap system and preserve private-route exclusions.

Use this for a public page that genuinely helps readers. Do not ask for hidden keyword blocks, fabricated reviews, or claims that a markup file guarantees AI recommendations. The page should answer a useful question and link to relevant next steps. Search metadata helps describe and discover the content; it cannot replace the content or establish a ranking outcome.

Acceptance: inspect the returned HTML, metadata, canonical, sitemap entry, and visible page. Check the mobile experience and ensure no overlay blocks the main text. Search indexing remains external and is not guaranteed. Keep the verification report precise about technical readiness instead of claiming a top position that cannot be established by publishing alone.

sections.heading: Prompt 16: write a maintenance handoff
paragraphs: Prompt: Create a concise handoff for the current working version. Explain the user workflow, record model, role rules, setup commands, configuration names, test steps, release path, rollback reference, and known limitations. Use facts from the repository and observed results. Separate completed behavior from planned work. Exclude private configuration values and avoid claiming tests that were not run.

Use this after a meaningful milestone or before another person takes over. A factual handoff reduces repeated investigation and keeps future prompts tied to the actual project. It can also reveal gaps: if nobody can explain which environment holds the records, that is a question to resolve before further expansion. Documentation is most useful when it describes the current system.

Acceptance: someone with appropriate project access can follow the note, identify the relevant code, and repeat the main check. Keep it short enough to maintain. A generated encyclopedia that becomes stale immediately is less helpful than a focused README and a small list of verified limitations. Update the handoff when the underlying behavior or release process changes.

sections.heading: Prompts 17–20: four focused follow-up patterns
paragraphs: Prompt 17, scope recovery: Inventory the current feature states as working, partial, demonstration-only, or untested. Identify the one unfinished step blocking the main user journey. Propose a bounded correction and defer unrelated feature work. Use this when repeated broad prompts have created many screens without a reliable action. Accept a plan that names the concrete blocker and preserves the last working version.

Prompt 18, regression prevention: Add a meaningful regression check for the observed duplicate-loan bug using the project's existing test patterns. Test the allowed case and the rejected overlap. Do not write a test that merely repeats the implementation. Use this after a real defect, where a stable test protects an important rule. Accept evidence that the test fails for the defect and passes for the correction where that can be established.

Prompt 19, cost clarification: Explain which parts of this feature consume building capacity and which use runtime services. Identify the relevant providers and current documented limits without guessing future traffic. Use a small, explicitly assumed workload example. Accept a clear model with uncertainty, not an invented exact monthly bill. This helps prevent a free prototype from silently depending on an unexamined paid service.

Prompt 20, targeted content change: Update the public page's explanation of the loan process to match the current supported behavior. Preserve its URL and design, remove unsupported claims, and link to the relevant guide. Verify the final rendered text and metadata. Use this when product behavior has changed and the marketing copy has fallen behind. Accept truthful current copy rather than a more dramatic promise.

sections.heading: A complete prompt sequence for a small booking app
paragraphs: Start with the planning prompt: Help me define a small workshop-booking app for a neighborhood craft studio. Visitors choose a session and reserve a place. Staff manage sessions and see reservations. The first release excludes payment and automatic calendar sync. Identify the minimum records, capacity rule, cancellation policy, and acceptance checks. Ask for the decisions that change the workflow before implementing code.

After reviewing the plan, use an implementation prompt: Build the session list and one complete reservation flow using fictional records and the selected persistence mechanism. Enforce capacity at the authoritative boundary. Show pending, full-session, validation, and failure states. Preserve form input after a failed save. Explain which behavior is real and which depends on configuration that is not yet available.

Then use a verification prompt: Test a successful reservation, the last available place, a repeated submission, and a full session. Verify that the staff roster matches accepted reservations. Check a fresh session and a phone layout. Report the actual version, environment, and results. Finally, ask for a focused correction for any failed case. The sequence separates product decisions, implementation, and evidence without requiring a separate prompt for every trivial styling choice.

sections.heading: Rewrite vague requests into observable changes
paragraphs: Vague: make the dashboard smarter. Better: the coordinator needs to see which sessions have unfilled places this week. Add a view based on authoritative session capacity and accepted reservations. Define the date range and time zone, exclude cancelled sessions, and provide a clear empty state. Verify the totals against a small fictional dataset. The revised prompt names a decision the dashboard should support.

Vague: fix authentication. Better: after a test user signs out, opening a private reservation link displays the previous participant's details until refresh. Expected: private details are unavailable immediately after sign-out. Reproduce the sequence, inspect session and cache handling, make a focused correction, and verify that a second test user cannot see the first user's record. The revised prompt provides a concrete failure without guessing its implementation cause.

Vague: make it rank first. Better: improve the public workshop guide so it answers how reservations work, includes current factual information, uses descriptive headings, has a stable canonical URL, and is linked from the relevant public pages. Verify meaningful HTML, metadata, and its sitemap entry. The revised prompt asks for work the builder can perform and verify, while leaving search ranking as an external outcome.

sections.heading: Use acceptance criteria that challenge the result
paragraphs: Acceptance criteria should include the case most likely to expose a mistaken assumption. If a feature filters overdue loans, include a returned loan with an old due date. If it limits records by organization, include two organizations with similarly named projects. If it counts available places, include a cancelled reservation. These examples test the meaning of the rule rather than only its most obvious successful case.

Keep the criteria understandable. Given a session with one available place, when two test requests compete for it, at most one is accepted and the other receives an accurate response. That statement can guide manual testing and an automated regression test without prescribing every implementation detail. The builder can select a suitable technical mechanism while remaining accountable for the observable result.

Avoid criteria that cannot be established in the current task. Perfect security, unlimited scale, and guaranteed search visibility are not useful pass conditions for a small build. Replace them with scoped requirements and relevant checks. State what remains outside the verification. A bounded, challenging acceptance test provides more confidence than a large list of vague assurances.

sections.heading: Decide when to ask for clarification
paragraphs: Clarification is useful when the answer changes the implementation materially. Whether members can view each other's loans affects the access model. Whether the primary button is blue or indigo usually does not. Tell the builder to resolve ordinary presentation choices using the existing design system while surfacing missing business rules. This keeps progress moving without letting important assumptions disappear.

Bundle related decisions. For a booking flow, ask about capacity, cancellation, time zone, and confirmation policy together. Explain the consequence of each choice in ordinary language. A nontechnical owner can make a good decision when the question describes the user outcome. A long series of implementation questions without context can make the project feel harder than it needs to be.

When you do not yet know the answer, choose a clearly labeled prototype assumption and test it where appropriate. For example, a demonstration may use one workshop time zone. Record that boundary and revisit it before a multi-region pilot. An assumption is manageable when it is explicit, narrow, and connected to a future check. It becomes dangerous when later prompts mistake it for an established product requirement.

sections.heading: A prompt review checklist before you press send
paragraphs: Read the prompt from the perspective of someone who has never seen the app. Can they identify the user, the next action, the relevant records, and the result? Have you named the existing project when it matters? Are examples fictional and appropriate? Does the request distinguish a required behavior from a visual preference? Remove unrelated ideas that would make the outcome difficult to verify.

Check for accidental scope expansion. A request to add a filter should not also replace login, change hosting, redesign the navigation, and add email. If those changes are all necessary, explain the relationship and ask for a staged plan. Otherwise, keep them separate. Focus makes both the implementation and the eventual review more useful.

Finally, name the evidence you need. For a text change, rendered copy may be enough. For a shared save action, verify persistence and the relevant access rule. For publishing, verify the intended version at the intended address. A prompt that ends with a clear acceptance check helps the builder report completion precisely and helps you recognize when work remains unfinished.

sections.heading: How to iterate when the answer is wrong
paragraphs: First determine whether the builder misunderstood the requirement or failed to implement an understood requirement. If the plan described the wrong workflow, correct the brief. If the plan was right but saving fails, provide reproduction steps and inspect the implementation. Repeating the original broad prompt often produces more variation without resolving the specific cause of the problem.

Keep a small evidence packet: starting version, action, expected result, actual result, and safe diagnostic context. Ask for the smallest change that addresses it. Recheck the original journey afterward. If a proposed solution changes unrelated parts, ask which evidence requires that expansion. Iteration works best when each prompt adds information rather than simply expresses stronger frustration.

Finally, recognize external blockers. An unavailable credential, unsupported runtime, missing repository permission, or pending store review cannot be repaired by rewriting a component. The builder should name the boundary and preserve the completed work. A precise prompt helps expose that distinction, while a precise acceptance check prevents an attractive response from being mistaken for a finished application.
